title: Learn Markdown from Scratch
subtitle: Format text for the web with plain characters
description: The formatting language of README files, notes, and chat. Learn headings, lists, links, and code blocks by writing them yourself.

lessons.title: Headings and Paragraphs
lessons.body:
Markdown turns plain text into formatted documents. You write with ordinary characters like `#`, `-`, and `*`, and a Markdown renderer turns them into headings, lists, and emphasis. It is used everywhere: GitHub README files, Reddit comments, Discord, notepad apps, and most documentation sites.

A heading starts with one or more `#` characters followed by a space. One `#` makes the biggest heading, two `##` the next size down, and so on to six:

```
# Big title
## Section
### Subsection
```

Paragraphs are the easiest part: just write a line of text, then leave a blank line before the next paragraph. No syntax needed.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a real reason people choose Markdown?
options: It is plain text that renders into formatted documents almost anywhere
It can only be written on Windows machines
It is a compiled programming language
exercises.explain: Markdown is portable plain text: readable as-is, and rendered into formatted output by countless tools.

exercises.prompt: Write the exact Markdown line for a level-1 heading that says: `Notes`
exercises.hint: One hash, one space, then the word.
exercises.explain: A single # followed by a space makes the biggest heading.

exercises.prompt: In the editor, write a level-2 heading called `Today`, followed by a paragraph that says: `I am learning Markdown`

patterns.m: a paragraph containing `I am learning Markdown`

exercises.hint: Two hashes for a level-2 heading, blank line, then the paragraph.
exercises.explain: `## Today` renders as a medium heading, and the plain line below it becomes a paragraph.

lessons.title: Bold and Italic
lessons.body:
Emphasis wraps words in marker characters. Wrap text in double asterisks for **bold**, single asterisks for *italic*:

```
This is **bold** and this is *italic* and this is ***both***.
```

Underscores work the same way: `__bold__` and `_italic_`. Most style guides pick asterisks and stick with them, because they cause fewer surprises when a sentence contains two words side by side.

One rule matters most: no spaces between the markers and the word they wrap. `** word **` will not render as bold.

exercises.prompt: Write the Markdown that shows the word `important` in bold

exercises.explain: Single asterisks around text make it italic.

exercises.prompt: Write one sentence that contains the word `bold` in bold and the word `italic` in italic, with any other words around them

patterns.m: the word bold wrapped for bold
the word italic wrapped for italic

exercises.solution: This word is **bold** and this one is *italic*.
exercises.hint: Double asterisks for bold, single for italic, no spaces inside the markers.

lessons.title: Lists
lessons.body:
Lists are the workhorse of Markdown. A bulleted (unordered) list starts each line with a dash, asterisk, or plus sign, followed by a space:

```
- Milk
- Bread
- Cheese
```

A numbered (ordered) list starts each line with a number and a dot:

```
1. Read
2. Practice
3. Rest
```

You can nest lists by indenting the sub-items with spaces (usually two to four):

```
- Fruit
  - Apples
  - Bananas
```

The renderer numbers ordered lists for you, so `1.`, `1.`, `1.` on every line still comes out as 1, 2, 3.

exercises.prompt: Which line correctly starts a numbered list item that says `Read`?
options: 1) Read is the only valid form
exercises.explain: `1. Read` with a number, a dot, and a space is the standard form.

exercises.prompt: Write the first line of a bulleted list item that says `Milk`
exercises.hint: A dash, a space, then the word.
exercises.explain: Any of -, *, or + followed by a space makes a bullet.

exercises.prompt: Make a bulleted shopping list with exactly three items: `Milk`, `Bread`, and `Cheese`

patterns.m: a line that is a bullet for Milk
a line that is a bullet for Bread
a line that is a bullet for Cheese

exercises.hint: Three lines, each starting with a dash and a space.

lessons.title: Links and Images
lessons.body:
A link is square brackets for the visible text, then round brackets for the address:

```
[Visit Example](https://example.com)
```

An image is exactly the same, with an exclamation mark in front. The square brackets hold the alt text, which describes the image for people who cannot see it:

```
![A friendly cat](https://example.com/cat.jpg)
```

That single `!` is the whole difference between a link and an image, so it is worth memorizing: brackets alone point somewhere, an exclamation mark first pulls a picture in.

exercises.prompt: Write a link whose visible text is `Search` and which points to `https://example.com`
exercises.hint: Square brackets for the text, round brackets for the URL.

exercises.prompt: What turns a link into an image?
options: Nothing, links and images are the same
exercises.explain: ![alt](url) embeds an image; without the ! it stays a link.

exercises.prompt: Write an image with alt text `A cat` pointing to `https://example.com/cat.jpg`, and below it a link with the text `Visit` pointing to `https://example.com`
exercises.hint: Image first with the !, then a blank line, then the link without it.

lessons.title: Code, Quotes, and Rules
lessons.body:
Inline code goes between single backticks, and it is the standard way to mention a command or filename inside a sentence: `npm install`.

A fenced code block uses three backticks on their own lines, and keeps everything inside exactly as written:

````
```
print("hello")
```
````

A blockquote starts a line with `>` and a space, which renders as an indented quotation:

```
> Be curious.
```

A horizontal rule is three dashes on their own line (`---`) and draws a dividing line. Tables exist too, built from pipes and dashes, but they are the least fun part of Markdown, so learn them the day you actually need one.

exercises.prompt: Which of these makes a fenced code block?
options: Three backticks on their own line
Three dots on their own line
exercises.explain: A fence is three backticks, once above the code and once below.

exercises.prompt: Write the command `npm install` as inline code
exercises.explain: Backticks make inline code, shown in a monospace font.

exercises.prompt: Write a blockquote that says `Be curious`, and below it a fenced code block containing the line `print("hi")`

patterns.m: a quote line starting with `> Be curious`
a fence line with three backticks
the code line print("hi") inside the fence

exercises.hint: Quote line with `> `, then blank line, then fence, code, fence.
